... to organize and understand biodiversity data.
Traditionally, biodiversity collections have depended on structured systems,
taxonomic classifications, controlled vocabularies,
cataloging standards, and carefully documented metadata.
But now we're introducing systems that work probabilistically.
Large language models can generate annotations, classifications,
descriptions, and links between datasets, often at a scale that would be
difficult for humans to achieve manually.
And that creates an interesting problem for large datasets like ours.
The question is no longer simply, can AI help us organize
biodiversity information? It becomes, how do we
govern the meaning that AI is creating?
There is a tremendous opportunity here.
AI can help enrich existing biodiversity records by generating or
suggesting metadata, identifying relationship between records, and
making collections easier to search and discover.
For example,
the Tulane University Biodiversity Research Institute Natural History Collection
contains millions of specimen records.
Much of the specimen information already exists, but it can be difficult to
connect that information that was created at different times by different
institutions or using different terminology.
AI can help identify those connections.
It can recognize that different descriptions refer to similar concepts.
It can suggest taxonomic relationships, extract information from
legacy records, or help researchers discover specimens that may
not find otherwise. In other words, AI has the
potential to act as a layer between biodiversity collections and the people trying
to use them. But that layer introduces a fundamental distinction.
AI can generate an answer without necessarily generating an
agreed-upon meaning, and that's where the challenge begins.
The first challenge is semantic ambiguity.
An AI system might produce an annotation that sounds perfectly reasonable to a
human reader but does not correspond cleanly to an existing biodiversity
concept or controlled vocabulary.
The second challenge is consistency.
Two AI systems, or even the same system at different times,
may describe the same specimen differently.
Probabilistic systems don't necessarily reproduce the consistency that we
expect from traditional cataloging systems.
Then there's provenance. If an AI-generated annotation enters a
biodiversity repository, we need to know where that information came
from. Was it extracted from the original specimen record?
Was it inferred by a model? Was it reviewed by a
curator? Was it subsequently modified?
And finally, there's institutional trust.
A biodiversity repository isn't simply a database.
It is a record of scientific knowledge.
When AI becomes involved in creating or transforming that knowledge,
institutions need to be able to understand what the system did and
why.
So the problem isn't necessarily that AI is unreliable.
The problem is that AI-generated knowledge can be difficult to interpret, trace,
and govern.
This brings us to knowledge organization.
Biodiversity informatics already has an important advantage.
Decades of work have gone into developing shared standards and semantic
frameworks.
Standards like controlled vocabularies, taxonomic authorities, and
established cataloging practices give us a common language for describing
biodiversity.
These systems provide something that generative AI does not automatically
provide: shared semantic commitments.
So rather than treating AI as a replacement for these systems, we can think about
AI as operating within them. An AI system might suggest
a classification or generate metadata, but the output can then be
mapped to established vocabularies, checking its community standards,
and accompanied by information about its provenance.
This suggests a model of AI-assisted curation rather than
AI-directed curation. That distinction is important.
The goal isn't to prevent machines from generating knowledge.
It's to make sure that machine-generated knowledge remains understandable and
accountable within the communities that maintain biodiversity infrastructure.
That means governance has to become part of the technical architecture.
We need to know not only what an AI system produced, but also
which vocabulary it used, what source information it relied
upon, what transformations occurred, and whether a human
curator reviewed the result.
In that sense, semantic governance becomes a bridge between artificial intelligence
and existing knowledge organization practices.
So where do we go from here?
We see an opportunity for biodiversity informatics communities, and
particularly organizations like TADWIG, to establish shared
practices for AI-augmented infrastructure.
First, AI-generated information should be provenance-aware.
We should be able to distinguish original observations from machine-generated
annotations and subsequent human revisions.
Second, AI output should be semantically transparent.
Where possible, generated concepts should be connected to recognized
vocabularies, standards, and identifiers.
Third, these systems need to be interoperable.
AI shouldn't create another layer of isolated terminology that makes it harder
to connect collections. Instead, it should help strengthen connections
between existing systems.
And finally, governance needs to be community-driven.
The standards community that already understands biodiversity data should have a
role in defining how AI systems interact with those standards.
The larger point is that AI changes more than the way we
process biodiversity data. It changes who and what
is participating in the organization of knowledge.
If we can build systems where AI-generated knowledge is traceable,
semantically grounded, interoperable, and open to human oversight,
then AI can become a powerful extension of existing biodiversity
infrastructures rather than a competing knowledge system.
For TADWIG, that creates an opportunity to help define not simply
how biodiversity data are exchanged, but how
AI-generated biodiversity knowledge becomes trustworthy, understandable,
and shareable.
